title: Emergence of a Shared Canonical Object Frame from In-the-Wild Videos
claim: Supervised methods need costly labels and per-category methods lack a shared frame; ours is label-free, scalable, and yields one shared frame.
layout: 3 panels: two stacked left priors, one right ours; checklist banners under each
description: The figure has three panels separated by dotted lines. The top-left panel, titled 'Supervised Category-Agnostic Methods' in green, shows human annotation, CAD models and canonical pose axes feeding an arrow into a neural network icon. The bottom-left panel, titled 'Self-Supervised Category-Level Methods' in purple, shows three video film strips (car, cart, chair) feeding separate Car and Chair model networks. The right panel, titled 'Our Method' in yellow, shows five film strips of different categories. They lead into a yellow box with three parts: noisy SfM camera pyramids in pink, a central geometric bottleneck cube, and aligned cyan camera pyramids, linked by curved arrows labeled self-supervised. Each panel ends with a gray banner of red crosses and green checks. The right panel's all-green checks draw the eye.
caption: Three approaches for learning of canonical object frames. Top left: Supervised methods can obtain a shared canonical frame from rendering aligned CAD models or manual pose annotation, which is expensive to scale. Bottom left: Self-supervised category-level methods learn from object-centric videos without canonical labels, but train separate models per category, limiting scalability and producing no shared frame across categories. Right: Our approach trains a single model across all categories by routing noisy SfM reconstructions through a shared geometric bottleneck, producing a shared canonical frame without canonical pose labels or category conditioning.
abstract: Comparing object orientations and positions across different instances requires their poses to be expressed in a shared canonical frame. Establishing such frames has traditionally required manual annotation, creating a scaling bottleneck that limits category and instance diversity. We show that a shared canonical frame can instead emerge from self-supervised training on object-centric videos of rigid objects captured in the wild, using only noisy camera poses from Structure-from-Motion. Our key idea is to route all training sequences through a shared geometric bottleneck: a coarse canonical mesh that carries no category-specific detail. By learning dense correspondences from image pixels to this mesh, and estimating per-sequence alignments from noisy SfM geometry, a common canonical frame emerges from multi-view consistency and the semantic priors of the feature extractor, without any canonical pose labels or category conditioning. Trained in a self-supervised manner on ${\sim}160{,}000$ in-the-wild object videos, our method achieves competitive accuracy on category-level pose estimation benchmarks compared to methods that rely on canonical pose supervision. The code and checkpoint are available on \href{https://github.com/Fischer-Tom/Emergent-Canonical-Frame/}{github.com/Fischer-Tom/Emergent-Canonical-Frame/}.
